passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of two cognitive training programs on reaction time in adults aged 20-30. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: a control group that received no training, Treatment A that involved a computer-based speed‑of‑processing task, and Treatment B that involved a mindfulness meditation protocol. After four weeks, participants completed a standardized reaction‑time task. The mean reaction times (in milliseconds) and standard deviations for each group were reported. The study aimed to determine whether the training programs could produce measurable improvements in processing speed and to quantify the magnitude of any observed effects. The authors also discussed potential mechanisms, such as neural plasticity and attentional resource allocation, that might underlie the observed changes. They concluded that Treatment A yielded the greatest improvement, while Treatment B (360 ms) and the control group (350 ms) showed no improvement.
table_data:
Condition | Mean Response Time (ms) | Standard Deviation
Control   | 350                     | 30
Treatment A | 300                     | 25
Treatment B | 360                     | 35
stem: Which condition had the lowest mean reaction time?

options.D: All conditions had the same mean

explanation: Treatment A had a mean of 300 ms, lower than Control (350 ms) and Treatment B (360 ms).
trap: Students assume the control group is the slowest baseline, but Treatment B (360 ms) had the highest mean, and Treatment A (300 ms) the lowest.

stem: Calculate Cohen’s d for the difference between Control and Treatment A.
explanation: Pooled SD = √[(30²+25²)/2] ≈ 27.6. Difference = 50 ms. Cohen’s d = 50/27.6 ≈ 1.81.
trap: Students divide the 50 ms difference by a single group's SD (30 gives 1.67; 25 gives 2.00) instead of the pooled SD of about 27.6.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT a valid conclusion from the data?

options.A: Treatment A had the lowest mean reaction time of the three conditions.
options.B: Treatment B is more effective than Control.
options.C: Treatment A has a large effect size.
options.D: Treatment B has a smaller effect size than Treatment A.

explanation: Correct: Treatment B's mean (360 ms) is slower than Control's (350 ms), so it is not more effective. Why the others are wrong: A) Treatment A's 300 ms is the lowest mean. C) Cohen's d for Control vs Treatment A is about 1.8, a large effect. D) Treatment B showed no improvement, so its effect is smaller than Treatment A's.
trap: Students assume any active training must beat the control, but Treatment B's mean (360 ms) was actually slower than Control (350 ms).
